html:
The Reinheitsgebot, or "purity order", is a law of 1516 from the duchy of Bavaria that said beer could be made only from water, barley and hops. Duke William IV issued it, and it also fixed the price of beer.

It is often called the oldest food law still in use, but that claim is loose. Towns such as Munich had similar rules before 1516, and today's German rules differ a good deal from the old text. Yeast was not listed because brewers did not yet know it was there; the foam from one batch simply started the next.

The law had practical aims. Keeping wheat and rye out of beer left them for bakers, and it banned odd additives used to flavour or strengthen beer. For centuries it applied only in Bavaria. Bavaria made it a condition of joining the new German Empire that the rule spread, and from 1906 it applied across Germany. It became part of the national image of German beer, linked with hops and lager brewing.
